platforms.title: It's Not the Heat Keeping You Up — It's These 3 Habits
platforms.meta_description: Struggling to sleep on hot nights? A cold shower before bed, late-night phone use, and afternoon coffee may be doing more damage than the heat itself.
platforms.body_html:
When a heatwave keeps you tossing and turning, it's tempting to blame the temperature alone. But three ordinary evening habits — a cold shower right before bed, scrolling on your phone in the dark, and an afternoon coffee — can each work against the natural drop in body temperature your brain needs to fall asleep. Untangling which habit is doing what makes it much easier to fix.

It's Not Just the Heat — Here's What's Really Happening

Falling asleep depends on your core body temperature dropping by roughly half a degree to a degree Celsius. On a hot, humid night that drop is already harder to achieve, and a cold shower taken right before bed can make it worse rather than better. Cold water triggers a sympathetic nervous system reflex called vasoconstriction — blood vessels near the skin narrow to hold heat in — which is the opposite of what your body needs to do to release heat and cool down for sleep. A 2019 meta-analysis in Sleep Medicine Reviews found that the timing and temperature of bathing matters far more than simply going cold.

Phone and laptop screens add a second layer to the problem. Research published in PNAS on evening use of light-emitting e-readers found that even a couple of hours of screen exposure before bed suppressed melatonin and pushed the circadian clock later, compared with reading a printed book. That delay compounds with heat that's already keeping your body temperature elevated.

Then there's the afternoon coffee. Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors, the same receptors that build up sleep pressure throughout the day. Its half-life averages around 5 hours, but can range from 1.5 to 9.5 hours depending on the person, according to sleep researchers cited by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine's Sleep Education program. A coffee at 3 p.m. can still leave roughly a quarter of its caffeine active in your system by 11 p.m., which is more than enough to delay sleep onset on a night that's already working against you.

Shift the Timing on All Three Habits

  • Move your shower earlier, or make it warm — showering with water around 40–42°C for about 10 minutes, 1–2 hours before bed, was the combination linked to falling asleep faster in the Sleep Medicine Reviews analysis. If a cold shower is the only way to cool off, take it well before your wind-down routine rather than right at bedtime.
  • Set a screen curfew 30–60 minutes before bed — put the phone in another room if possible, and lower the brightness rather than relying on a night-mode filter alone.
  • Stop caffeine 8–10 hours before your bedtime — for a bedtime around 11 p.m., that generally means no coffee after early-to-mid afternoon.

None of this means giving up your evening shower or afternoon coffee for good — shifting the timing is usually enough. If sleeplessness continues on most nights for more than two weeks, or shows up alongside dizziness, a racing heartbeat, or confusion that could point to heat exhaustion, it's worth checking with a doctor rather than waiting it out. This article is for general information only and isn't medical advice.
